This publication reports for the first time the physiochemical, the intrinsic mechanical properties and the seed effect of anomalous Al-substituted 11 Å tobermorite synthesized via the innovative supercritical hydrothermal flow process at 400 ◦C and 25 MPa. This approach allows synthesizing highly crystalline tobermorite fibers in only 8 s, with characteristics very close to the natural tobermorite. The anomalous 11 Å tobermorite exhibits aluminosilicate chains with a high polymerisation degree and a less defective structure compared to materials produced via the conventional hydrothermal method. ## 1. Introduction

Natural tobermorite mineral was discovered in 1880 in Tobermory (Scottland), hence its name. Natural tobermorite is considered as a rare and scarce mineral that crystallizes in the form of plates or flat fibres. In nature, it is commonly found in or nearby cavities of basic rocks, or at the contact between dolerite and limestone, or granodiorites [1]. The structure of tobermorite is complex, and consequently, its description has been, for many years, a matter of debate [1,2].

Depending on the degree of hydration (i.e. content of water mole­ cules), the basal distance ranges from 9 Å, to 11 Å or 14 Å. As a consequence, three structural varieties of tobermorite exist, 9 Å tober­ morite, 11 Å tobermorite or 14 Å tobermorite, that differ for their d002 values in the diffraction patterns, 9.3, 11.3 or 14.6 Å, from the least to the most hydrated type, respectively. It has been observed by X-ray diffraction that upon heating at 100 ◦C, 14 Å tobermorite transforms into 11 Å tobermorite, which in turn can give rise to 9 Å tobermorite by a further dehydration process at 300 ◦C. However, some natural samples of 11 Å tobermorite, labelled anomalous, contrarily from those labelled normal, despite the heating treatment, preserves their structure without any change in the basal distance value [3].

Furthermore, in nature, the formation of tobermorite usually occurs with the presence of aluminum, or in rarer cases, other elements (Mg, Fe, or Na) as a partial substitution of Si in its structure. Al-substituted tobermorite is considered as the crystalline model for calcium alumi­ nosilicate hydrate (C-(A-)S-H), the glue in Portland cement concrete containing various supplementary cementitious materials, and it has also been found in ancient Roman concrete [4,5]. In that case, the for­ mation of Al-substituted tobermorite is associated with the pyroclastic pozzolans, a Si-poor and Al-rich specie, used in the Roman concrete binders.

If compared to modern structures, the service life of Roman struc­ tures is around two orders of magnitude longer [6], and their high durability (over 2000 years) has been related to the presence of Al-tobermorite and C-(A-)S-H [5,7,8]. In this context, the investigation of the mechanical properties of this synthetic C-(A-)S-H model com­ pound is of high interest. High-pressure X-ray diffraction is also a powerful technique to determine the stability of C-(A-)S-H-based phases for comparison between different C-(-A)S-H phases with similar structures.

The synthesis of 11 Å tobermorite is much more complicated than that of other calcium silicate hydrate phases, due to its low stability at high temperature and thus to the difficulty in manufacturing a crystal­ line and pure single phase material [9]. It has been stated that the lower stability at high temperature is due to the lower degree of polymerisa­ tion, in terms of condensation of Si-tetrahedra, if compared with xonotlite, a more stable calcium silicate hydrate phase with Ca/Si= 1 [10].

The most investigated synthesis parameters in the hydrothermal production of 11 Å tobermorite are temperature, pressure, type of pre­ cursors, and pH of the precursor solution. For each parameter, a wide range of values has been explored, making it difficult to ascertain the optimal conditions for synthesising this material.

A preliminary study on the thermal stability of tobermorite, reported by Speakman, has shown that below 100 ◦C, only amorphous C-S-H phase can form, while above 140 ◦C crystalline synthetic tobermorite transforms into xonotlite [11]. Furthermore, the xonotlite/tobermorite boundary region depends, apart from the temperature, on several other experimental parameters, such as the Ca/Si ratio, the pressure and the Al/Si ratio. The higher the pressure and the Al/Si ratio are (up to 200 MPa and Al/(Al + Si) molar ratio equal to 0.15, respectively) and

the lower the Ca/Si ratio is (down to 0.8), the more stable the tober­ morite is [12]. However, when comparing the synthesis parameters to determine the better conditions at which tobermorite is stable, another variable should be taken into account: the duration of the synthesis. In fact, the higher the temperature, the lower should be the time to avoid the transformation into xonotlite.

It appears clear that only an accurate control of the reaction/crys­ tallization can promote the formation of pure single-phase tobermorite and inhibit the formation of other mineral phases. That control is challenging to achieve in a traditional batch method, where the mild temperatures commonly used involve either the formation of other stable phases or a very long synthesis time. For these reasons, a meth­ odology that allows to curtail the synthesis times and captures more truthfully the tobermorite formation process that takes place in nature is needed.

The supercritical hydrothermal flow synthesis (SHFS) meets these requirements. The main advantage of this methodology is related to the ultra-fast reaction kinetics, which allows the synthesis of minerals in only a few seconds [13-16]. Furthermore, in addition to the reduced synthesis times, the synthetic minerals are characterised by high crys­ tallinity and purity, compared to their natural counterparts that are often mixed with other phases or impurities. SHFS allows producing model nanominerals by mimicking natural environments at high tem­ peratures and pressures, and thus offers the opportunity to describe their structures and the correlated intrinsic properties rigorously. The pro­ duction of tobermorite exploiting the supercritical water-based tech­ nology was first reported in 2017 [13,17]. However, in these studies, the investigation of the properties as well as the applications of the mineral were limited by the trace amount. With the aim of exploring the use of crystalline tobermorite as seeds in cement paste, in this work, a more suitable set-up for a flexible and effective production was designed and developed.

The great interest in investigating the effect of tobermorite on the nucleation and further growth of hydration product in cement paste is related to the lack in the existing literature, contrarily to the extensive studies for semicrystalline C-S-H [18-21,4,7]. The most relevant works on the investigation of tobermorite seeding effect were reported by Land et al. [22] and Diez-Garcia et al. [23]. While the first has shown the acceleration of the hydration process of white cement (type CEM I) by adding natural minerals, the second has explored the effect of tober­ morite synthesized by subcritical hydrothermal synthesis (215 ◦C for 4 h). In both cases, the seeding effect was studied with a calorimetric analysis to investigate the different heat exchanges in the cement pastes prepared with two minerals, tobermorite and xonotlite. Although both materials produced an acceleration of the early hydration kinetic, the effect of xonotlite was much stronger. This effect has been explained by Land et al. by taking into account the different morphological properties of the two types of CSH particles. In fact, the diameters and the specific surface areas were 0.42 µm and 280 mm2/g for xonotlite and 0.63 µm and 198 mm2/g for tobermorite, respectively [22]. In a later study, it has been reported that semicrystalline C-S-H seeds with a higher Ca content (Ca/Si = 2) exhibit a faster nucleation and, thus, acceleration effect than seeds with lower Ca content (Ca/Si = 0.4) [24]. However, these mate­ rials were mixed with some impurities (portlandite and/or silica gel), which could also influence early hydration and result in a distorted evaluation of the real quantity of C-S-H additions. Consequently, the influence of the Ca/Si ratio of seeds on the cement hydration is still not fully elucidated. As a consequence, it appears clear the importance of continuing investigating the effect of crystalline calcium silicate hydrate nanoparticles as seeds in cement paste to fill the gaps in knowledge. Furthermore, it should be mentioned that semicrystalline C-S-H

## 2. Materials and methods

2.1. Materials

11 Å tobermorite was synthesized by supercritical hydrothermal flow synthesis [23]. As described above, due to the instability of this mineral phase at high temperature, a small quantity of Al was employed to stabilize the crystal structure. The precursors solutions were prepared by dissolving a stoichiometric amount of calcium nitrate tetrahydrate (Ca(NO3)2 ⋅ 4 H2O), sodium metasilicate nonahydrate (Na2SiO3 ⋅ 9 H2O), and aluminium nitrate nonahydrate (Al(NO3)3 ⋅ 9 H2O) in deionized (DI) water in order to have bulk Ca/(Al+Si) = 0.83 and Al/(Al+Si) = 0.15 molar ratios. During the synthesis, the precursor solutions were kept under a N2 flow to avoid sample carbonation. The precursor solutions were delivered using two Jasco Isocratic HPLC pumps with a total combined flow rate of 16.5 mL/min. The precursors were mixed in a T-mixing piece located at the inlet of the reactor. The reactor itself consists of a 0.74 m length stainless steel pipe with a diameter of 9/16 in. The external diameter is equal to 14.29 mm and the internal one to 4.78 mm, corresponding to a total reactor volume of 1.33 × 10⁻⁵ m³ . The production of 11 Å tobermorite (~ 1.4 g/h at M = 0.05 mol/L) was performed in an in-house user-customised set-up as aformentioned using supercritical water as solvent. The system was regulated to maintain a stable temperature of 400 ± 5 ◦C and a pressure of a pressure of 250 ± 2 bar, with a back- pressure regulator set to 250 bar, ensuring consistent pressure conditions. This corresponds to a Reynolds number of 243 in the synthesis conditions (with density=112.33 kg/m3 and viscosity= 3.39e-5 Pa.s from the NIST database). Under these conditions, the residence time should be as fast as possible to avoid the formation of other species, as xonotlite, but long enough to allow the crystallisation of the material. In this work, to meet the needs for the production of highly crystalline tobermorite, a residence time of 8 s was used [26,27]. The as-synthesized sample was filtered and then dried in an oven at 60 ◦C overnight to obtain a dry powder.

### 2.2. Methods

2.2.1. X-ray diffraction

Powder X-ray diffraction patterns of 11 Å tobermorite were recorded on a PANalytical X’Pert PRO MPD X-ray diffractometer in Bragg- Brentano θ-θ geometry. A Cu Kα radiation, consisting of Kα1 (λ = 1.5406 Å) and Kα2 (λ = 1.5444 Å) lines, with a weighted average wavelength of 1.5418 Å, operating at a generator voltage of 45 kV and a current of 40 mA, was employed as radiation source. The spectra were recorded in the 8.012–99.991◦(2θ) range with a minimum step size of 0.017◦(2θ) by a X’Celerator multi-strip detector.

HP-XRD experiment was performed at the beamline 12.2.2 of the Advanced Light Source (ALS) at the Lawrence Berkeley National Labo­ ratory. A BX-90 diamond anvil cell was used in an axial geometry. The culet diameter of the diamond pair was 400 μm. A cylindrical chamber with diameter of ~110 μm and thickness of ~90 μm was drilled on a

stainless-steel gasket using a laser milling machine. Over half volume of the chamber was loaded with densely packed Al-tobermorite. Then, a ruby sphere (α-Al2O3 doped with 0.05 wt% Cr3+) was loaded into the chamber. The ruby was used as a gage for applied hydrostatic pressure in the chamber. Subsequently, the chamber was filled with a methanolethanol solution (4:1 by volume) as the pressure-transmitting medium and sealed immediately. The incident X-ray beam energy was 25 keV (wavelength = 0.4959 Å and beam size = ~30 μm). 2D diffraction im­ ages were collected by a MAR345 image plate then integrated into 1D diffraction patterns. Unit cell parameters were refined using CelRef, with Merlino’s tobermorite structure of B11m space group [28].

2.2.2. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM)

The size and the morphology of tobermorite particles synthesized under supercritical conditions were investigated by SEM. The analyses were performed with Jeol JSM 6360 A operating in a voltage range of 0.4 – 40 kV. Prior to measurement, the sample was placed in an aluminium stub by using a two-sided carbon tape, and to increase its conductivity, an electrically grounded layer of gold was deposited on it by employing a sputter coater equipment.

2.2.3. High resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM)

First, tobermorite particles were dispersed in ethanol, and then the resultant solution was subjected to ultrasonication at ambient temper­ ature for ~15 min, before being dried onto a carbon coated copper grid. High resolution images were acquired using a JEOL Jem 2200FS FEG microscope. The instrument operated at a voltage of 200 kV, making accessible magnification between 4000 × and 600000 × , with a spatial resolution of 0.1 nm.

2.2.4. Solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance

Solid-state 29Si nuclear magnetic resonance (29Si SSNMR) measure­ ment was carried out on a 300 MHz Bruker Avance spectrometer equipped with a 7.05 T wide-bore magnet. The experiment was per­ formed at room temperature using a standard 4-mm magic angle spin­ ning (MAS) probe with MAS rates of 30 kHz. A 45◦excitation pulses with a short length of 2.4 µs and a recycle delay of 30 s were used. 29Si chemical shifts are given relative to silicon oil at −22 ppm.

To identify the aluminium coordination structures, solid-state 27Al nuclear magnetic resonance (27Al SSNMR) analysis was performed on a 500 MHz Bruker Avance spectrometer equipped with a 11.7 T wide-bore magnet. In that case, a short pulse of a length of 1µs corresponding to a selective π/12 pulse was applied with a recycling delay of 1 s. 27Al chemical shifts are referenced relatively to Al(NO3)3 at 0 ppm.

2.2.5. Raman spectroscopy

The vibrational properties of Al-tobermorite were investigated through Raman micro-spectroscopy, employing a HORIBA Jobin-Yvon Xplora spectrometer. The set-up was equipped with a laser of excita­ tion wavelength equal to 532 nm and spot size ~1 µm. The measurement used a 50 × objective, gratings with 1200 lines/mm and a CCD detector. The spectra were acquired with an exposition of 10 s and 10 accumu­ lations in the 200 – 1200 cm−1 range.

2.2.6. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy

A Bruker Equinox 55 spectrophotometer was employed to perform Fourier transform infrared measurement. The sample spectrum was recorded over 32 scans, with a spectral resolution of 4 cm−1 within the 400–4000 cm−1 absorption range. To carry out the analysis, the sample (9 mg) was mixed with KBr (100 mg), being this compound optically transparent within the mid-IR region.

2.2.7. Calorimetry

Cement pastes were prepared with ASTM Type I cement at a waterto-cement mass ratio (w/c) of 0.5 at 25 ◦C. In the case of seeded pastes, tobermorite particles (0.5 wt% or 1 wt% per weight of cement) were

## 3. Results and discussions

3.1. Crystal structure and physicochemical properties of tobermorite

Powder X-ray diffraction was used to identify the mineral phase and to investigate the crystallinity of tobermorite synthesized in supercriti­ cal water. In Fig. 1(a), PXRD pattern shows well-defined peaks coinci­ dent with those reported in the PDF file no. 00–0831520 for orthorhombic 11 Å tobermorite in the International Centre for Diffrac­ tion Data (ICDD) database. The most intense diffraction peak of the pattern is centred at 7.8◦(2θ) which corresponds to a basal distance d002 = 11.4 Å, in agreement with what reported for natural 11 Å tobermorite specimens [1,32,33]. It must be emphasised that we are synthesising

tobermorite at a temperature (400 ◦C) far above its stability limit, which is approximately 140 ◦C [34]. The successful synthesis of crystalline, phase-pure and stable Al-substituted 11 Å tobermorite under supercrit­ ical conditions (400 ◦C, 250 bar) is related to the unique physico­ chemical properties of supercritical water (SCW). Compared to ambient conditions, supercritical water (SCW) undergoes drastic changes in po­ larity, dissociation behavior, and flow properties; all of which have a direct impact on the solubility, reactivity, and crystallization of pre­ cursor species during synthesis. One major factor is the significant drop in water dielectric constant. At room temperature, water has a high dielectric constant (ε ≈78.5), which makes it a good solvent for polar and ionic compounds. However, under supercritical conditions, the dielectric constant drops sharply to around 5.9 at 400 ◦C and 250 bar. This evolution induces a drastic reduction of the solubility of metal salts and silicate species. As a result, when the precursors (calcium nitrate, sodium metasilicate, and aluminum nitrate) are introduced into SCW, they become immediately supersaturated, triggering fast nucleation and precipitation of a solid phase of 11 Å tobermorite. This rapid transition from dissolved to solid state minimizes the time available for competing phases as xonotlite to form and favors direct crystallization of the desired tobermorite structure. This behavior is also predicted by the Born theory, where a lower dielectric constant decreases the equilibrium constant for ionic solubilization, pushing the system toward precipitation.

As presented above, normal tobermorite specimen dehydrates to the 9 Å form when heated at 300 ◦C. On the other hand, despite the anomalous variant dehydrates under similar conditions, its basal dis­ tance does not decrease [1,3,34]. To study the nature of our 11 Å Al-tobermorite, either normal or anomalous, the sample synthesized in supercritical water was further subjected to dehydration at 300 ◦C in an oven for 24 h. As shown in Fig. 1(b), after the thermal treatment the basal peak (002) has not shifted, suggesting that via SHFS we have synthesized 11 Å anomalous tobermorite. The behaviour of anomalous tobermorite upon dehydration has been correlated by Mitsuda et al. to the existence of cross-linkages of silicate layers across the interlayer, which prevents a reduction in the interlayer space when water mole­ cules are lost [3,35]. Furthermore, recently Dupuis et al., proposed a structural model, according to which the most distinctive feature of the normal and anomalous varieties of tobermorite relies on the presence or absence of zeolitic calcium cations in the cavities [35]. Because of this structural hypothesis, the zeolitic Ca cations of normal tobermorite would be coordinated to oxygen atoms from the silicate chains and from water molecules. Thus, due the heating and water molecules lost, Ca ions can only coordinate to silicate chain oxygen, and the generated electrostatic forces are adequate to depolymerize the bridging sites and bring the layer collapse, reaching the equilibrium distance at about 9 Å. In anomalous tobermorite, however, no zeolitic Ca cations exist in the cavities; consequently, proper calcium re-coordination does not occur by dehydration (i.e., no severe structural rearrangement occurs).

The morphology of tobermorite crystals was investigated by SEM and HR-TEM. As shown in Fig. 2(a), (b), and (c), the mineral phase continuously synthesized in supercritical water exhibits a fiber-like morphology with approximately 2 – 20 µm in length and 10 – 20 nm in width. This result confirms the similarity of the tobermorite prepared in supercritical water to the natural mineral, which also crystallizes in the form of fibers or plates [36]. On the contrary, tobermorite synthe­ sized by conventional hydrothermal synthesis shows a foil-like morphology unless templates are used to induce fiber formation [36, 37].

To explain these findings, we should consider the kinetic effects: the formation of natural tobermorite occurs at low temperature, due to its unstable character, over many years, while synthetic varieties have to form in a much shorter time. As a result, the reaction temperature must be increased in the laboratory to trigger a faster crystallisation process. However, at higher temperature, only an accurate control on the reac­ tion time can inhibit the formation of other mineral phases. That control

Fig. 3(a) and (b) show the well-ordered arranged lattice of the material, where different atomic planes can be distinguished. Thanks to high-resolution imaging, the interlayer distance between calcium layers was determined being approximately 11.4 Å, Fig. 3(c), in agreement with the value, 11.3 Å, reported for natural specimens [1,32]. The aluminosilicate structure of Al-substituted tobermorite was investigated by SSNMR, which is an excellent technique to obtain in­ formation on the polymerisation degree of the chains. The 29Si MAS NMR spectrum of Al-tobermorite is shown in Fig. 4(b). The conventional Qn(mAl) nomenclature was used to indicate silicate tetrahedra con­ nected via oxygen to n adjacent tetrahedra (SiO4 or AlO4), m of which are Al sites and the remaining n-m Si sites.

The deconvolution of the spectrum in six components was performed to obtain quantitative information on the content of silicon and

aluminium ions in sites with different connectivities. First, a signal centred at −79.6 ppm was detected and assigned to Q1 sites. This contribution is commonly related to end-of-chain silicon tetrahedra, thus indicating a defective silicate chain structure. The low value of this contribution, only 4 %, implies a high degree of polymerisation related to the presence of long silicate chains in Al-tobermorite synthesized via SHFS. It is worth mentioning that the fraction of end-of-chain silicon Q1

found in our sample is much lower than what previously reported, 14–17 %, for other synthetic Al-tobermorite obtained by conventional hydrothermal synthesis [17,41].

Two more broad signals appear at −92.3 and −96.4 ppm, assigned to chain cross-linking sites Q3(1Al) and Q3(0Al), respectively. The presence of Q2(1Al) confirms that Al3+ is present in the bridging tetrahedra po­ sitions. However, the fraction of Q2, 40 %, is higher than Q2(1Al), 33 %, implying that these sites allocate a higher number of Si atoms than Al atoms. The replacing of silicon atoms (Si4+) by aluminium atoms (Al3+) generates in the structure a negative charge excess, which is expected to be compensated by Ca2+ cations placed in the interlayer or by single proton.

Interestingly, the addition of aluminium in the mineral structure gives rise to alumina cross-linking sites, which can be detected by the presence of Q3(2Al) at −88.8 ppm. The L¨owenstein’s rule states that –Al–O–Al-bond formation should be forbidden. However, violations of that rule have been documented in several systems, such as mica [42], zeolite [43], and calcium aluminosilicates [44], when the Al content is sufficiently high. Furthermore, the presence of Q3(2Al) has been detected in natural Al-tobermorite [35] as well as in Al-tobermorite in ancient Roman seawater concrete [5]. Consequently, Dupuis et al. pro­ posed that the L¨owenstein’s rule might be circumvented under some kinetic constraints [35], which could be the case of the formation of Al-tobermorite under supercritical conditions.

## 4. Conclusions

The present study investigates the physiochemical and intrinsic mechanical properties of anomalous Al-substituted 11 Å tobermorite synthesized via an innovative hydrothermal flow process in supercritical water at 400 ◦C and 25 MPa. The main advantage for using SHFS methodology relies on boosted reaction kinetics, allowing the synthesis of high crystalline tobermorite fibers in only 8 s. The in-depth charac­ terisation analysis has shown that, despite the curtail of reaction times, the synthetic material is very close to the natural mineral in crystallinity and morphologies. Furthermore, by using techniques as SSNMR and Raman, we have shown that 11 Å tobermorite exhibits aluminosilicate chains with high polymerisation degree, a less defective structure if compared to samples produced via conventional hydrothermal method. These findings suggest that this innovative technology more accurately captures the formation process of minerals that takes place in nature.

Furthermore, the intrinsic mechanical properties of Al-tobermorite synthesized in supercritical water were investigated here for the first time by HP-XRD. We have found that this material is characterised by higher incompressibility along the b-axis and bulk modulus K0 than what is commonly observed for other synthetic tobermorite. The study of the mechanical properties provides information for predicting the mineral’s long-term behaviour, relevant in applications concerning the design of cement-based materials with Al-tobermorite.

Later, the autocatalytic formation of C-S-H gel induced by the seeds addition have been proved by calorimetry and microtomography ana­ lyses. Tobermorite particles act as nucleation points to trigger the quick formation of the hydration product in cement paste.

In this context, our exhaustive study could have implications in developing a greener and ultra-fast synthesis methodology for produc­ ing CSH mineral seeds for applications to the ready-mix concrete industry.

A B S T R A C T

In blended cement systems, the principal hydration product is calcium (alumino) silicate hydrate (C-(A-)S-H). The investigation into how aluminum incorporation affects its mechanical properties is essential for optimizing the formulation and properties of cementitious materials. This study employs high-pressure X-ray diffraction to explore the intrinsic mechanical properties of nanocrystalline single-chain C-A-S-H (Ca-to-Si ratio 1.6), resem­ bling chemical compositions of C-A-S-H in blended cement systems. Increasing aluminum incorporation softens all unit cell axes, with basal planar incompressibility governed by the aluminum coordination number, showing an increasing order of Al(IV) < Al(VI) < Al(V). The softening of the basal plane arises from the longer Al–O bond length relative to Si–O bond, and the different distortion indexes in AlOx polyhedra. The hydrogen bond numbers and angles relative to the basal plane within per unit cell influence the basal planar incompressibility of single-chain C-A-S-H. Aluminum-uptake-induced expansion in basal space contributes to a softened c-axis.

## 1. Introduction

Portland cement (PC), a primary binder of modern concrete, ac­ counts for approximately 8 % of global CO2 emissions and 7 % of energy use [1–3]. During modern concrete production, to enhance concrete durability and reduce production costs, supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) are commonly incorporated as partial substitutes for PC [4,5]. Widely adopted SCMs, mainly consisting of amorphous (alu­ mino) silicates, are derived from industrial residues such as ground granulated blast-furnace slag [6] and coal fly ash [7], along with poz­ zolans which have abundant global natural reserves [8].

Calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H), as the principal hydration product of PC, is critical to binding the solid phases of concrete components together. C-S-H in hardened PC pastes exhibits a Ca-to-Si molar ratio (Ca/Si ratio) ranging from 0.6 to 2.0 [9], with a prevalent range of 1.7 to 2.0 in conventional formulations [10]. When PC is partially substituted with aluminum-containing SCMs, aluminum uptake in C-S-H’s (alu­ mino)silicate chain leads to reduced calcium content, forming calcium aluminosilicate hydrates (C-A-S-Hs) [11]. In hardened blended PC

pastes, the Ca/Si ratio of C-A-S-Hs can decrease to approximately 1.4–1.6, depending on the chemical composition, pozzolanic reactivity, and the amount of SCMs added [12,13]. At Ca/Si > 1.25, the (alumino) silicate chains exhibit a lower polymerization degree, with more vacant bridging sites relative to C-S-H containing less calcium. Excessive Al is the driving force to secondary mineral precipitation, e.g., str¨atlingite (in blended cement systems and synthetic C-A-S-Hs) and katoite (in syn­ thetic C-A-S-Hs) [14]. Consequently, even when the aluminum is highly concentrated—either in blended PC paste or synthetic pure single pha­ se—the Al-to-Si molar ratio (Al/Si ratio) of C-A-S-H remains limited to approximately 0.1 [15–17]. This type of C-(A-)S-H, also termed C-(A-)S- H(I), owns a higher structural ordering than C-S-H formed in hardened blended PC pastes at the nanometer scale, evidenced by X-ray diffraction [18]. Single-chain C-(A-)S-H(I) synthesized under ambient conditions resembles defective 14 Å tobermorite in terms of nanostructure, featuring a CaO7 sheet flanked on “dreierketten” (alumino)silicate chains and interlayer water containing charge-compensating cations, see Fig. 1 (A) [19,20]. High aluminum con­ tent (typically Al/Si above 0.05) favors the formation of pentahedrally and octahedrally coordinated aluminum, Al(V) and Al(VI). Neverthe­ less, the aluminum positions for the three coordination environments within the C-A-S-H molecular structure remain a subject of ongoing debate. It has been suggested that Al(V) may reside either within the interlayer regime or at bridging positions, functioning as a chargecompensating component [21,24–26], and Al(VI) is structurally incor­ porated into the nanostructure or resides within the interlayer [27], or appears as an unknown aluminate hydrate phase (third aluminate hy­ drate) [21,23,28].

Mechanical properties are among the most important indices of concrete, and most of the literature has extensively explored the me­ chanical properties (typically hardness, Young’s moduli, and creep moduli) of synthetic and hydrated C-(A-)S-Hs from multiple length scales (macro to micro) [29–33]. Nanoindentation measurements at the microscale have demonstrated that mechanical responses of C-(A-)S-Hs are closely associated with their internal packing density and pore structure [34–37]. Hitherto, improvements in the mechanical perfor­ mance of concrete have been nearly completed down to the micro scale by fining the pore structure of concrete [38]. A detailed evaluation of C- (A-)S-H mechanical behavior at the nanometer scale is essential to advancing the performance optimization of hardened concrete mate­ rials. As shown in Fig. 2, high-pressure X-ray diffraction (HP-XRD), assisted by synchrotron radiation, enables the in-situ application of hydrostatic pressures up to several tens of gigapascals (GPa), using hard X-rays with a typical wavelength of approximately 0.5 Å. This synchrotron-based HP-XRD has been proven to be one of the most effective and promising methods for investigating the intrinsic me­ chanical properties of natural minerals and (nano)crystalline binding phases because the hydrostatic compression conditions eliminate the influence of mesoscale porosity—gel pores, inter-hydrate pores, and capillaries—thereby isolating the response of the crystal lattice itself [39–42]. Recent HP-XRD investigations on C-S-Hs have demonstrated that increasing the Ca/Si ratio (0.8–1.3) leads to an enhancement in its intrinsic bulk modulus [43,44], in contrast with the well-known unva­ lidated nanoscale “defect-driven” hypothesis, which proposes that increasing Ca/Si ratio softens the phase due to a higher fraction of bridging site vacancies that disrupt the silicate chains and decreases structural ordering [45]. This increased bulk modulus is attributed to interlayer densification, not to silicate chain connectivity. With an increasing Ca/Si ratio, the interlayer space tends to be narrower but more Ca-enriched, leading to a higher intrinsic bulk modulus given comparable basal planar incompressibility [43,44,46].

Aluminum incorporation introduces greater complexities to both the nanostructure and nanomechanical behavior of C-S-H [47]. This incor­ poration generally increases C-A-S-H’s intrinsic mechanical properties by modifying its atomic structure and densifying its interlayer. HP-XRD studies demonstrated that the intrinsic bulk modulus of double-chain C (-A)-S-H increases from 50 ± 2 GPa for C-S-H(I) toward 64 ± 3 GPa as for Al/(Al + Si) of 0.05, and further to 71 ± 3 GPa as for Al/(Al + Si) of 0.1 [41]. This stiffening effect is controlled by the Al-induced dreier­ ketten chain crosslinks, formed at high temperature, e.g., 80 ◦C, which act as nanostructural columns that resist the interlayer contraction under compressive loads [19,41]. The presence of these crosslinks de­ creases the interlayer spacing from 12.2 Å for Al-free single-chain C-S-H to 11.5 Å for double-chain C-A-S-H, thereby increasing c-axial incom­ pressibility. In the basal plane (also termed ab plane), aluminum incorporation strengthens the double-chain C-A-S-Hs through the higher number of charge-compensating calcium cations and stronger hydrogen bonding [41]. Al-tobermorite, serving as a representative structure of C- A-S-H, has also attracted surging attention to its chemical properties and intrinsic mechanical properties [48–50]. An increase in aluminum incorporation leads to enhanced incompressibility along the basal plane in double-chain tobermorite, ranging from approximately −1/280 GPa−1 at Al/(Al + Si) = 0 to −1/245 GPa−1 at Al/(Al + Si) = 1/6, due to the higher concentration of charge-compensating calcium ions and stronger hydrogen bonding. In contrast, single-chain Al-free tobermorite exhibits slightly higher basal planar incompressibility (−1/293 and −1/ 322 GPa−1 along the a and b axes, respectively) than the double-chain counterparts, attributed to enhanced steric constraints in the inter­ layer of single-chain Al-free tobermorite. Along the c-axis, the incom­ pressibility of double-chain tobermorite remains from −1/225 to −1/ 250 GPa−1 and is largely unaffected by aluminum incorporation. How­ ever, single-chain tobermorite shows a significantly lower c-axial incompressibility (−1/150 GPa−1), due to the absence of crosslinks [41]. In addition, we have demonstrated a negative or negligible influ­ ence of aluminum incorporation on the incompressibility of the basal plane for 11 Å double-chain tobermorite, which structurally resembles double-chain C-A-S-H [19,41]. The oxygen atom shared at the crosslinking sites functions like a hinge, allowing the bonded atoms, e.g., Si and Al, to rotate around it. Rather than compressing bonds of covalent nature, such as Si-O-Si/Al, that span interlayer regimes, the hinge structure accommodates stress through bond reorientation, which is energetically more favorable [41,51]. These experimental findings highlight the importance of aluminum uptake in C-S-H in nano­ mechanical properties, paving the way to optimize macroscopic me­ chanical properties and to reduce cementitious materials creep through a bottom-up strategy. In this study, the molecular structure and nanoscale mechanical properties of single-chain C-(A-)S-Hs, resembling those formed in blended PC systems, with Ca/Si of 1.6 and Al/Si of 0.05 and 0.1, were characterized. The atomic and nanometer structure of single-chain C-A-S-Hs is compared with theo­ retical calculations and stable Al-rich crystalline minerals, e.g., katoite (Ca3Al2(OH)12), gibbsite (Al(OH)3), and andalusite (Al2SiO5). The in­ fluences of polyhedral distortion and Al–O bond length induced by aluminum incorporation on the incompressibility along all three axes in each unit cell are unveiled. The results are impactful on the material design of concrete and subsurface well cementing using a bottom-up approach and are useful to the validation of theoretical calculations and to the development of new force fields.

## 2. Materials and methods

2.1. Materials

Single-chain C-(A-)S-Hs were prepared with a target Ca/Si ratio of 1.6 and target Al/Si ratios of 0, 0.05, and 0.1 in the initial mixture. Precisely weighed stoichiometric quantities of CaO (derived from calcined CaCO3), fumed SiO2 (Aerosil 200, Evonik), and CaO⋅Al2O3 were homogenized into Milli-Q water at a water-to-solid mass ratio of 45 under a nitrogen atmosphere. The single-chain C-(A-)S-Hs slurries were cured at 20 ◦C for 365 days to ensure near-equilibrium conditions were attained prior to further processing [16]. Previous studies have shown that aluminum incorporation typically stabilizes within 182 days, with minimal changes thereafter, particularly under high Ca/Si ratios where

the low silicate content and elevated pH accelerate reaction kinetics [16,52]. Each slurry was vacuum filtered through 0.45 μm nylon membranes, sequentially washed with water-ethanol solution (1:1 vol­ ume ratio) and pure ethanol, followed by freeze-drying across 168 h to remove excess water and minimize the risk of carbonation [53]. The dry powders were conditioned at 30 % relative humidity in nitrogen-purged desiccators and subsequently vacuum-sealed for storage prior to anal­ ysis. More detailed compositions in the molar ratio of the synthetic single-chain C-A-S-H structures are summarized in Table 1. The C-A-S-H, which only contains Al(IV) with the initial Al/Si = 0.1 and Ca/Si = 1.6, was synthesized for a reference in XANES experiments. A reference C-A- S-H(I) was aged at 80 ◦C in a Teflon vessel for 90 days to achieve the equilibrium [54]. The filtration, drying, and storage followed the iden­ tical experimental procedures as for single-chain C-A-S-Hs. Details regarding the thermodynamic and kinetic behavior of aluminum incorporation, along with the quantitative phase analysis of the syn­ thesized C-(A-)S-H, are available in [52]. It is worth noting that although the actual Al/Si ratio of the sample with a nominal Al/Si = 0.10 is only 0.06, it still serves as a representative composition. This corresponds to a 20 % increase compared to the Al/Si = 0.05 sample, which is chemically meaningful given the limited aluminum uptake capacity at high Ca/Si ratios. At Ca/Si = 1.6, aluminum incorporation is significantly restricted due to the scarcity of bridging Q2 sites and the tendency to form sec­ ondary calcium aluminate hydrate phases [52].

2.2.1. X-ray diffraction

High-pressure XRD experiments on single-chain C-(A-)S-Hs were performed at the BL 12.2.2 (superbend) in the Berkeley Lab’s Advanced Light Source. The diamond culet used in the experiment had an approximate diameter of 400 μm. Cylindrical sample chambers, approximately 90 μm thick and 100 μm in diameter, were created by laser machining through a rhenium gasket. 2.2.2. Raman spectroscopy

Raman spectra of single-chain C-A-S-Hs were collected by placing

powder samples onto a clean glass slide and analyzing at 1800 grooves/ mm grating (Horiba LabRAM). Prior to each measurement, the spec­ trometer was aligned using the 520.7 cm−1 silicon reference peak to maintain measurement precision. Raman spectra were acquired at ambient temperature in a backscattering configuration, using a 632.8 nm laser as the excitation source. A 50× objective lens was employed to focus the laser onto the specimen, achieving a spot diameter below 1 μm.

2.2.3. NMR

Solid-state 27Al NMR spectra of single-chain C-A-S-Hs were acquired at 300 MHz (Bruker Advance), functioning under a magnetic field (7.05 T), i.e., 27Al Larmor frequency (78.204 MHz). The spectra were acquired with a conventional 4 mm MAS probe spinning at 10 kHz. Chemical shifts were externally calibrated using an aluminum nitrate reference solution. A short pulse duration of 1.3 μs, equivalent to a selective π/12 pulse optimized using aluminum nitrate solution, was applied. Recycle delays (0.5–5 s) were selected based on the specific sample characteristics.

Spectral fitting was carried out using Dmfit, a commercial software package, with a mixed Lorentzian–Gaussian profile applied. The line shapes were constrained by setting the Lorentzian-to-Gaussian ratio to 0.5 and limiting the full width at half maximum to below 3 ppm. Throughout the fitting process, chemical shift positions were fixed for each component, and peak intensities were restricted accordingly.

2.2.4. XANES

Single-chain C-A-S-H, reference C-A-S-H (only containing Al(IV)), gibbsite, and katoite were measured using XANES at station II of the PHOENIX beamline, Swiss Light Source. A monochromatic beam was generated by a planar grating monochromator. The X-ray beam was collimated to a square spot measuring 500 μm × 500 μm. Powder samples were spread in thin layers onto indium foil and subsequently fixed to a copper holder. This holder was placed on the sample stage inside a vacuum chamber. XANES measurements were acquired in fluorescence-yield mode using a single-element silicon drift detector equipped for energy-dispersive analysis.

3.2. Nanostructure at high pressure and intrinsic mechanical properties

*Fig. 7 presents the diffractograms of single-chain C-(A-)S-Hs recor­ ded under varying applied hydrostatic pressures at room temperature. With elevated hydrostatic pressure, the diffraction peak positions exhibit a consistent rightward shift, indicating a progressive decrease in interlayer spacing. For instance, the (002) peak displays decreased dspacing under compression, reflecting the contraction of the interlayer regime. At high hydrostatic pressures, most C-(A-)S-H diffraction peaks exhibit noticeable broadening, attributed to pressure-driven amorph­ ization (i.e., loss of structural ordering) [40]. Given that full width at half maximum (FWHM) can reflect both crystallite size and lattice strain [72,73], we plotted the pressure-dependent evolution of FWHM to further investigate the origin of this broadening. As shown in Fig. 8, a clear linear relationship was observed, indicating that microstrain is the dominant contributor. This level of correlation is commonly regarded as acceptable in HP-XRD analyses of cementitious materials [74]. Such behavior is frequently reported in HP-XRD investigations, extending to various other cementitious phases beyond C-(A-)S-H [75–77]. The amorphization is more profound for single-chain C-A-S-H with Al/Si of 0.1, particularly the (002) peak, at elevated hydrostatic pressure, indi­ cating a reduced stability as well as ordering of nanostructures with aluminum uptake at the atomic-to-molecular scale.*

In single-chain C-(A-)S-H, incompressibility along all unit axes is determined based on the Biot strain response under varying hydrostatic compressive loads. For a single-chain nanostructure, the a- and b-axial

values are −1/400 and − 1/385 GPa−1, respectively (see Fig. 9), both marginally exceeding values previously reported for samples synthe­ sized at ambient conditions with lower Ca/Si ratios (0.8–1.4) [44]. The increase in basal planar incompressibility of single-chain C-S-H with a higher Ca/Si ratio (i.e., 1.6 here) results from the higher amount of Ca occupancy in the interlayer (more CaOH+ replaces Ca2+) [44]. The basal planar incompressibility of single-chain C-(A-)S-Hs decreases with the increase in Al/Si ratios from 0 to 0.1. This observed trend can be explained by two reasons: firstly, with the increasing aluminum content, the softer Al–O bond and greater angular distortion of AlOx in C-A-S-H result in a less compressible basal plane. This phenomenon can be explained by the longer Al–O bond (from 1.78 Å to 2.02 Å, depending on the aluminum coordination number) of single-chain C-A-S-Hs in comparison with the Si–O bond (in the range of 1.6 Å −1.66 Å) of C-S- H [78]. Secondly, the aluminum polyhedron in alumino-silicate chains also leads to a soft basal plane. Assuming that the single-chain C-A-S-Hs contains 100 SiO4 sites, the 27Al NMR results suggest that, in the sample with Al/Si of 0.05, the number of Al atoms in Al(IV), Al(V), and Al(VI) are approximately 0.95, 1.75, and 2.3, respectively. For the sample containing aluminum the most, e.g., Al/Si = 0.1, these values increase to 5, 1.7, and 2.5, respectively. The numbers of Al(V) and Al(VI) remain comparable between the two single-chain C-A-S-H samples. This normalized representation is intended solely to facilitate intuitive comparison of the relative abundances of different aluminum coordi­ nation states, and does not reflect the actual stoichiometry or structural unit of C-A-S-H. Therefore, the observed decrease in incompressibility of the basal plane can be mainly assigned to the negative influence of Al (IV).

Here, we continue to discuss how pentahedral and octahedral Al affect the incompressibility along the ab direction. Aluminum incorpo­ ration into the aluminosilicate chains of single-chain C-A-S-H is the key factor causing a pronounced change in basal planar incompressibility, as evidenced by the decreasing a- and b-axis incompressibility shown in Fig. 9. It has been well established that Al(IV) enters the chain by substituting for Si at the bridging sites [35,59]. If Al(V) and Al(VI) are also accommodated at the bridging sites of the aluminosilicate chains, their structures would likely be [AlO2(OH)4]5−, [AlO2(OH)4-x(H2O)x]5-x, or [AlO(ØH)(OH)4]6−for Al(VI), and [AlO2(OH)3]4−for Al(V) [27]. The ØH denotes a Brønsted acidic hydroxysilicate linkage, specifically rep­ resented as Al-OH-Si. None of the aforementioned four structural con­ figurations can stabilize as a hinge structure (Q3), which has been demonstrated to significantly decrease the basal planar mechanical properties in 11 Å Al-free double-chain tobermorite and double-chain C- A-S-Hs [41,51]. The absence of Q3 species is primarily evidenced by our Raman results (Fig. 4), showing no detect­ able Q3 signals. This fact also implies a higher likelihood for terminal hydroxyl groups to form hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) with coordinating oxygen [83], which may influence the basal planar incompressibility. Fig. 10 shows the spatial distribution of hydrogen bonds within each unit cell of single-chain C-A-S-H(I). Al (IV) tetrahedron exhibits the highest number of hydrogen bonds, pri­ marily due to its minimum basal spacing (13.49 Å) and shortest Al(IV)-O bond length (1.7886 Å), resulting in a more compact structure that promotes hydrogen bond formation. Aluminum incorporation may also alter the Ca–O bond, the primary bond in C-A-S-H, thereby affecting the basal planar mechanical prop­ erties. Richardson summarized 859 Ca–O bond lengths from 35 crys­ talline C-S-H minerals and related minerals, identifying the most probable Ca–O bond length as ranging from 2.3 to 2.4 Å [84], see Table 7. The average Ca–O bond lengths of C-A-S-Hs are approximately 0.10 Å longer than those of related crystalline minerals. High-pressure X-ray diffraction measurements reveal that the incorporation of aluminum into single-chain C-S-H(I) increases its compressibility of all axes in comparison with the Al-free counterpart with equal Ca/Si ratio. The softened basal plane of single-chain C-A-S-H is attributable to the longer Al–O bond (compared to Si–O bond), the longer Ca–O bond (induced by aluminum uptake) and the more dis­ torted Al polyhedron (induced by aluminum uptake) compared to the C- S-H with the same Ca/Si ratio. The c-axial softening found in singlechain C-A-S-Hs can be ascribed to an expanded interlayer resulting from aluminum incorporation. The intrinsic bulk moduli of single-chain C-A-S-Hs (52–53 GPa) are lower than single-chain C-S-H with Ca/Si of 1.6 (81 GPa), primarily due to the softening at the basal plane caused by aluminum incorporation into the non-crosslinked aluminosilicate chains via substitution for bridging-site Si.

For the first time, our work reveals the influences of three different aluminum coordination numbers on the intrinsic mechanical properties of single-chain C-A-S-H with a high Ca/Si ratio, 1.6. Our single-chain C- A-S-Hs with three different aluminum contents contain comparable amounts of pentahedral and octahedral aluminum, but the amount of Al (IV) shows the largest variation. The high Al(IV) amount results in a softened basal plane of single-chain C-A-S-Hs. The basal planar incom­ pressibility increases following this order: Al(IV) < Al(VI) < Al(V), due to the Al–O bond type and distortion index of aluminate polyhedron, as well as the hydrogen bond number and angle per unit cell of single-chain C-A-S-H. The Al(IV)-O(Si) bond, being the shortest, results in the stiffest basal plane in Al(IV)-containing C-A-S-H, while the longest bond, Al(V)- O(H), leads to the softest basal plane in Al(V)-containing nanostructure. With a moderate Al(VI)–O(H) bond length, the basal planar incom­ pressibility of containing Al(VI) C-A-S-H falls between that of C-A-S-H containing Al(IV) and Al(V). The basal planar incompressibility is highly sensitive to the second-nearest neighbors of aluminum in the nano­ structure. The most distorted Al(V) results in the most compressible basal plane, followed by Al(VI), while the least distorted Al(IV) results in the most incompressible basal plane. The greatest number of hydrogen bonds per unit cell of Al(IV)-containing C-A-S-H corresponds to the stiffest basal plane. The contribution of hydrogen bonding to basal planar incompressibility is greater in Al(VI)-containing C-A-S-Hs than in those containing Al(V), aligning with the order for basal planar incom­ pressibility: Al(IV) > Al(VI) > Al(V).

This study unveils the nano-mechanical characteristics of singlechain C-A-S-H(I), forging a clear relationship between atomic

configuration and incompressibility along each unit cell axis. Our find­ ings lay a scientific foundation for improving the use of Al-rich sup­ plementary cementitious materials through a mechanistic understanding of how the coordination chemistry of aluminate in­ fluences the nano-mechanical properties of blended Portland cement systems. By integrating high-pressure X-ray diffraction experiments with multiple spectroscopic techniques, our findings pave the way to the bottom-up material design approach through tailoring cementitious materials, enabling precise control over creep-related deformation and mechanical performance. These results contribute to the fundamental comprehension of nanostructure and mechanical property relationships of single-chain C-A-S-H and provide a robust framework for designing low-carbon concrete and well cementing with superior mechanical sta­ bility, ultimately guiding the development of more sustainable cemen­ titious systems.
